Topic 08·Ashraf Sir · Lectures 1–2

DTFT and DFT

From the Fourier series to N-point DFTs, reading bins, and the DFT's properties.

1 past question on this topic

Four transforms, one square

One structural rule generates every Fourier-type transform. We already know the left column; this topic derives the right one: what happens to Fourier's idea when time arrives in samples.

time is continuoustime is discrete
periodicFourier series (CTFS)DFS / DFT
aperiodicFourier transform (CTFT)DTFT

Discrete in one domain ⇔ periodic in the other. Sampling time makes the spectrum periodic; sampling frequency (keeping only NNN bins) makes time periodic.

Sampling as an impulse train

The coefficients are NNN-periodic. Sampling in time made the spectrum periodic. Only NNN unique values exist; we keep the window k=0,1,…,N−1k=0,1,\dots,N-1k=0,1,…,N−1.

Reading the bins: where the negative frequencies went

The natural spectrum is centred at k=0k=0k=0, with negative kkk on the left. Periodicity moves each negative-kkk coefficient into the window: c−k=cN−kc_{-k}=c_{N-k}c−k​=cN−k​. The negative side is not lost; it folds onto the upper bins.

How to read NNN bins. Bins 0→N20\to\frac N20→2N​: positive frequencies, low → high. Bins N2→N−1\frac N2\to N-12N​→N−1: negative frequencies, high → low. A real low-pass signal peaks at k=0k=0k=0 and near k=Nk=Nk=N, and dips at k=N2k=\frac N2k=2N​.

The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)

For a length-NNN sequence {x[n]}n=0N−1\{x[n]\}_{n=0}^{N-1}{x[n]}n=0N−1​, define the transform as the bare analysis sum, written with the twiddle factor

WN≜e−j2πN,WNN=1 (an N-th root of unity; its powers cycle).W_N\triangleq e^{-j\frac{2\pi}N},\qquad W_N^N=1\ (\text{an }N\text{-th root of unity; its powers cycle}).WN​≜e−jN2π​,WNN​=1 (an N-th root of unity; its powers cycle).  X[k]=∑n=0N−1x[n] WNkn,k=0,…,N−1x[n]=1N∑k=0N−1X[k] WN−kn,n=0,…,N−1 \boxed{\,X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]\,W_N^{kn},\quad k=0,\dots,N-1\qquad\qquad x[n]=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X[k]\,W_N^{-kn},\quad n=0,\dots,N-1\,}X[k]=n=0∑N−1​x[n]WNkn​,k=0,…,N−1x[n]=N1​k=0∑N−1​X[k]WN−kn​,n=0,…,N−1​

Three bridges:

  • X[k]=N akX[k]=N\,a_kX[k]=Nak​: the DFT is the DFS, rescaled;
  • ck=1T0X[k]c_k=\frac1{T_0}X[k]ck​=T0​1​X[k]: the CTFS coefficients of the sampled signal xp(t)x_p(t)xp​(t);
  • X[k]=X(ejω)∣ω=2πk/NX[k]=X(e^{j\omega})\big|_{\omega=2\pi k/N}X[k]=X(ejω)​ω=2πk/N​: samples of the DTFT (Part III).

We never needed the continuous signal. The DFT formula only consumes the NNN numbers x[0],…,x[N−1]x[0],\dots,x[N-1]x[0],…,x[N−1]; nothing in it remembers TsT_sTs​ or x(t)x(t)x(t). Any list of numbers (an audio buffer, a pixel row, a sensor log) has a DFT. The sampling story was scaffolding.

Part I in one picture: NNN points in time ⇄ NNN points in frequency, with DFT one way and IDFT the other.

Part II — the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform

Now let the signal be aperiodic

Take an aperiodic x(t)x(t)x(t) restricted to an interval of length T0T_0T0​. Sampling gives a finite sequence, non-zero only for 0≤n≤N−10\le n\le N-10≤n≤N−1:

xp(t)=∑nx[n] δ(t−nTs).x_p(t)=\sum_nx[n]\,\delta(t-nT_s).xp​(t)=n∑​x[n]δ(t−nTs​).

An aperiodic signal calls for the Fourier transform. Take the CTFT of the impulse train; each impulse sifts:

Xp(jΩ)=∑n=−∞∞x[n]e−jΩnTs.X_p(j\Omega)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x[n]e^{-j\Omega nT_s}.Xp​(jΩ)=n=−∞∑∞​x[n]e−jΩnTs​.

Now relabel the frequency axis by the sampling period, ω=ΩTs\omega=\Omega T_sω=ΩTs​. The same spectrum becomes the DTFT:

 X(ejω)≜Xp(jΩ)∣ΩTs=ω=∑n=−∞∞x[n] e−jωn \boxed{\,X(e^{j\omega})\triangleq X_p(j\Omega)\Big|_{\Omega T_s=\omega}=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x[n]\,e^{-j\omega n}\,}X(ejω)≜Xp​(jΩ)​ΩTs​=ω​=n=−∞∑∞​x[n]e−jωn​

ω\omegaω is digital frequency, in radians per sample. For the length-NNN capture the sum runs over n=0,…,N−1n=0,\dots,N-1n=0,…,N−1.

Winding picture. For a segment of x(t)=1+cos⁡6tx(t)=1+\cos6tx(t)=1+cos6t on 0≤t≤1.50\le t\le1.50≤t≤1.5 s, nothing repeats outside it, so the winding runs over the whole segment and every rate ω\omegaω gets its own value: a continuous spectrum. Sampled with Ts=124T_s=\frac1{24}Ts​=241​ s, the 3 Hz tone becomes 6⋅124=π46\cdot\frac1{24}=\frac\pi46⋅241​=4π​ radians per sample: consecutive points are turned by the same angle ω\omegaω.

The DTFT is 2π2\pi2π-periodic

Each term repeats every 2π2\pi2π, since e−j2πn=1e^{-j2\pi n}=1e−j2πn=1 for integer nnn:

X(ej(ω+2π))=X(ejω).X(e^{j(\omega+2\pi)})=X(e^{j\omega}).X(ej(ω+2π))=X(ejω).
  • Any 2π2\pi2π-wide window holds one full period; the usual principal interval is [−π,π][-\pi,\pi][−π,π].
  • [π,2π)[\pi,2\pi)[π,2π) is the folded copy of [−π,0)[-\pi,0)[−π,0).
  • In physical units, [−π,π][-\pi,\pi][−π,π] corresponds to [−Ωs2,Ωs2]\left[-\frac{\Omega_s}2,\frac{\Omega_s}2\right][−2Ωs​​,2Ωs​​] with Ωs=2πTs\Omega_s=\frac{2\pi}{T_s}Ωs​=Ts​2π​ (revisited in Sampling).

The inverse DTFT

Same pattern as Part I, but the spectrum is a continuous function of ω\omegaω, so we integrate over one 2π2\pi2π period instead of summing NNN bins. Substitute the analysis sum and swap sum and integral:

12π∫2πX(ejω)ejωndω=∑mx[m] 12π∫−ππejω(n−m)dω=x[n],\begin{aligned}&\frac1{2\pi}\int_{2\pi}X(e^{j\omega})e^{j\omega n}d\omega\\[6pt]&= \sum_mx[m]\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{j\omega(n-m)}d\omega\\[6pt]&= x[n],\end{aligned}​2π1​∫2π​X(ejω)ejωndω=m∑​x[m]2π1​∫−ππ​ejω(n−m)dω=x[n],​

because complete cycles integrate to zero: 12π∫−ππejωrdω=1\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{j\omega r}d\omega=12π1​∫−ππ​ejωrdω=1 if r=0r=0r=0 and 000 otherwise.

 x[n]=12π∫2πX(ejω) ejωn dω \boxed{\,x[n]=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{2\pi}X(e^{j\omega})\,e^{j\omega n}\,d\omega\,}x[n]=2π1​∫2π​X(ejω)ejωndω​

x[n]x[n]x[n] is a continuum superposition of ejωne^{j\omega n}ejωn over one period, versus the DFS, a finite sum of NNN of them.

Part III — the DFT through the DTFT lens

The DFT samples the DTFT

Look at the DFT definition: it is the DTFT evaluated at the discrete frequencies ω=2πNk\omega=\frac{2\pi}Nkω=N2π​k. Nothing to derive:

X[k]=∑n=0N−1x[n]e−j2πNkn=X(ejω)∣ω=2πNk.\begin{aligned}&X[k]\\[6pt]&= \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j\frac{2\pi}Nkn}\\[6pt]&= X(e^{j\omega})\Big|_{\omega=\frac{2\pi}Nk}.\end{aligned}​X[k]=n=0∑N−1​x[n]e−jN2π​kn=X(ejω)​ω=N2π​k​.​

One transform, two views. Periodic view: Fourier-series coefficients. Aperiodic view: NNN samples of the DTFT. Same NNN numbers.

Zero-padding: same spectrum, finer samples

Append zeros to a length-NNN sequence to reach length M≥NM\ge NM≥N. The zeros add nothing to the DTFT sum, so the spectrum is unchanged, but the MMM-point DFT samples it at spacing 2πM\frac{2\pi}MM2π​ instead of 2πN\frac{2\pi}NN2π​:

XM[k]=∑n=0M−1x[n]e−j2πMkn=X(ejω)∣ω=2πMk.\begin{aligned}&X_M[k]\\[6pt]&= \sum_{n=0}^{M-1}x[n]e^{-j\frac{2\pi}Mkn}\\[6pt]&= X(e^{j\omega})\Big|_{\omega=\frac{2\pi}Mk}.\end{aligned}​XM​[k]=n=0∑M−1​x[n]e−jM2π​kn=X(ejω)​ω=M2π​k​.​

More pixels, not more information. Zero-padding interpolates the picture of the same DTFT; it cannot resolve what the NNN real samples never captured.

Back to physical frequency, and to hertz

The DTFT axis was normalised, ω=ΩTs\omega=\Omega T_sω=ΩTs​. Undo it for bin kkk:

\end{aligned}$$ - Bins $0\dots\frac N2$ span $0\dots\frac{f_s}2$; bins $\frac N2\dots N-1$ span $-\frac{f_s}2\dots0$, i.e. $f_k=(k-N)\frac{f_s}N$. - One $2\pi$ period of the DTFT is one $f_s$ of physical frequency. - This is exactly the ordering numpy.fft.fftfreq reports, and why spectrum tools show $0$ to $\frac{f_s}2$. **Example:** $N=8$ samples at $f_s=8$ kHz gives $\Delta f=1$ kHz per bin. ```fig dft-hz ``` **Frequency resolution is the reciprocal of the record length**, $\Delta f=1/T_0$: to resolve two tones 1 Hz apart you need at least one second of data. ### The same derivation in Lathi's notation (CSE 311) Approximate $G(f)=\int_0^{T_0}g(t)e^{-j2\pi ft}dt$ by a Riemann sum with step $T_s$ and evaluate at $f=qf_0$:

G_q=\sum_{k=0}^{N_0-1}g_k,e^{-jq\Omega_0k},\qquad g_k=T_sg(kT_s),\quad\Omega_0=2\pi f_0T_s=\frac{2\pi}{N_0},\quad f_0=\frac1{T_0}.

$f_0=1/T_0$ because sampling the spectrum at spacing $f_0$ makes the time signal periodic with period $1/f_0$, and that period must be the record length $T_0$ so that copies do not overlap. # Part IV — DFT properties ## Everything lives on a clock The DFT only ever sees $N$ numbers, and synthesis rebuilds them $N$-periodically. So indices live on a clock: define

((n))_N\triangleq n\bmod N,\qquad\text{e.g. }((9))_8=1,\ ((-1))_8=7 .

```fig dft-clock ``` Tiling the $N$ samples forever gives the **periodic extension** $\tilde x[n]=x[((n))_N]$. It matches $x[n]$ on $0,\dots,N-1$ and is the copy the DFT really works with. **Nothing falls off the end of $N$ points; it wraps.** Every shift becomes a rotation of the clock. ## Two properties for free - **Linearity.** $a\,x[n]+b\,y[n]\leftrightarrow a\,X[k]+b\,Y[k]$ (both sequences of length $N$; pad the shorter with zeros first). - **Periodicity.** $W_N^{(k+N)n}=W_N^{kn}$, so $X[k+N]=X[k]$: the bins live on the same clock as the samples. **The one proof move:** substitute into the DFT sum, re-index, and let the clock absorb whatever spills past the edge. Since both $\tilde x[n]$ and $W_N^{kn}$ are $N$-periodic, any $N$ consecutive terms give the same sum. ## Circular time shift Shift the periodic extension by $m$ and substitute $r=n-m$: $$\begin{aligned}&\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\tilde x[n-m]W_N^{kn}\\[6pt]&= W_N^{km}\sum_{r=-m}^{N-1-m}\tilde x[r]W_N^{kr}\\[6pt]&= W_N^{km}X[k].\end{aligned}$$ The window slid to $r=-m,\dots,N-1-m$, but any $N$ consecutive terms give the same total.

x[((n-m))_N]\ \leftrightarrow\ W_N^{km}X[k]=e^{-j\frac{2\pi}Nkm}X[k].

$|W_N^{km}|=1$: a shift changes no magnitude, only phase. Where a signal sits in time lives entirely in the phase of $X[k]$. ## Frequency shift (modulation) Multiply by a complex tone in time and the spectrum rotates:

W_N^{-k_0n}x[n]=e^{j\frac{2\pi}Nk_0n}x[n]\ \leftrightarrow\ X[((k-k_0))_N].

Special case $k_0=\frac N2$: $e^{j\pi n}=(-1)^n$. Flipping every other sign slides the spectrum by half the clock, so low and high frequencies trade places. ```fig dft-modulation ``` ## Time reversal and conjugation Reversal plays the clock backwards ($0$ stays, $1\leftrightarrow N-1$, $2\leftrightarrow N-2$, …). Substitute $r=-n$ and slide the window:

x[((-n))_N]\ \leftrightarrow\ X[((-k))_N]=X[N-k].

Conjugating the sum flips the kernel, $(W_N^{kn})^*=W_N^{-kn}$:

x^[n]\ \leftrightarrow\ X^[((-k))_N]=X^*[N-k].

### Real signals: conjugate symmetry If $x$ is real then $x^*=x$, so its DFT must equal the conjugation result:

\boxed{,X[N-k]=X^*[k],}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad |X[N-k]|=|X[k]|\ (\text{even}),\quad\angle X[N-k]=-\angle X[k]\ (\text{odd}).

Two symmetries about $k=\frac N2$. Only bins $0,\dots,\frac N2$ are free; the upper half mirrors them. Check on $\{1,2,3,4\}$: $X[3]=-2-2j=X^*[1]$. Corollary: real **and** even $\tilde x$ gives a real $X[k]$. ```fig dft-symmetry ``` This is why the fold picture works: bin $N-k$ is bin $k$'s negative-frequency partner. ## Parseval's relation

\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|x[n]|^2=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}|X[k]|^2 .

*Proof:* replace $x^*[n]$ by the conjugated IDFT and swap the sums: $$\begin{aligned}&\sum_nx[n]x^*[n]\\[6pt]&= \sum_nx[n]\frac1N\sum_kX^*[k]W_N^{kn}\\[6pt]&= \frac1N\sum_kX^*[k]\underbrace{\sum_nx[n]W_N^{kn}}_{X[k]}\\[6pt]&= \frac1N\sum_k|X[k]|^2 .\end{aligned}$$ Check on $\{1,2,3,4\}$: time side $1+4+9+16=30$; bin side $\frac{100+8+4+8}{4}=30$. ✓ The $N$ tones $W_N^{-kn}$ are orthogonal, so the DFT is a change of basis: it re-books energy, never creates or destroys it. ## The property table | property | time domain | DFT domain | |---|---|---| | linearity | $a\,x[n]+b\,y[n]$ | $a\,X[k]+b\,Y[k]$ | | circular time shift | $x[((n-m))_N]$ | $W_N^{km}X[k]$ | | modulation | $W_N^{-k_0n}x[n]$ | $X[((k-k_0))_N]$ | | time reversal | $x[((-n))_N]$ | $X[((-k))_N]$ | | conjugation | $x^*[n]$ | $X^*[((-k))_N]$ | | real signal | $x[n]$ real | $X[N-k]=X^*[k]$ | | duality | $X[n]$ (bins replayed as a signal) | $N\,x[((-k))_N]$ | | circular convolution | $(x\circledast h)[n]$ | $X[k]H[k]$ | | multiplication | $x[n]h[n]$ | $\frac1N(X\circledast H)[k]$ | | Parseval | $\sum_n\lvert x[n]\rvert^2$ | $\frac1N\sum_k\lvert X[k]\rvert^2$ | # Part V — filtering with the DFT ## Why convolution matters An LTI system is completely described by $h[n]$, and its output is the **linear** convolution $y[n]=\sum_mx[m]h[n-m]$. Lengths add: $L$ input samples and $M$ taps give $L+M-1$ outputs, at a direct cost of about $L\cdot M$ multiplications. **The dream:** in every Fourier world so far, convolution in time became multiplication of spectra. If that held for the DFT, filtering would be: transform, multiply $N$ numbers, transform back. Does it hold? *Almost.* ## What multiplying DFTs actually does Take two length-$N$ sequences, multiply their DFTs bin by bin, and invert: $$\begin{aligned}&y[n]\\[6pt]&= \frac1N\sum_kX[k]H[k]W_N^{-kn}\\[6pt]&= \sum_{m=0}^{N-1}x[m]\underbrace{\frac1N\sum_kH[k]W_N^{-k(n-m)}}_{\text{IDFT of }H\text{ at }n-m}.\end{aligned}$$ But $n-m$ can be negative, and the IDFT evaluated off the grid returns the periodic extension, $\tilde h[n-m]=h[((n-m))_N]$:

\boxed{,y[n]=\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}x[m],h[((n-m))_N]=(x\circledast h)[n]\ \leftrightarrow\ X[k]H[k],}

This is almost convolution, but the index into $h$ wraps around the clock. **Multiplying DFTs convolves circularly.** ## Circular vs linear, step by step Running pair: $x=\{2,4,5,6,5,3,2,1\}$ ($L=8$), $h=\{1,2,1\}$ ($M=3$). **Linear at $n=0$:** flipping $h$ puts taps at $m=0,-1,-2$. $x$ only exists for $m=0,\dots,7$, so the off-edge taps multiply nothing: $$\begin{aligned}&y[0]\\[6pt]&= 1\cdot x[0]+2\cdot x[-1]+1\cdot x[-2]\\[6pt]&= 2 .\end{aligned}$$ **Circular at $n=0$:** indices are read on the clock, $((-1))_8=7$ and $((-2))_8=6$. The off-edge taps are not dropped; they **wrap** to the right and multiply the other end of $x$: $$\begin{aligned}&y[0]\\[6pt]&= 1\cdot x[0]+2\cdot x[7]+1\cdot x[6]\\[6pt]&= 2+2+2\\[6pt]&= 6 .\end{aligned}$$ **Equivalently, extend $x$ to the left:** the wrapped values are exactly what the periodic extension puts at $m=-1,-2$. Going round the wheel is walking along the unrolled $\tilde x$; the sliding $h$ grabs the previous lap's tail. ```fig dft-unroll ``` **Worked comparison.** - Linear (length $8+3-1=10$): $\{2,8,15,20,22,19,13,8,4,1\}$. - Circular (length 8): $\{6,9,15,20,22,19,13,8\}$. Six values agree; the first two are corrupted, one per off-edge tap. Circular convolution is the linear result **folded mod $N$**: $6=2+4$ and $9=8+1$. This is **time aliasing**. ```fig dft-circ-vs-linear ``` ## Zero-padding makes it linear If the linear result fits inside $N$ points, nothing folds: > **The zero-padding rule.** Pad both sequences to length $N\ge L+M-1$; then circular convolution equals linear convolution. Padded to $N=10$, the previous lap now ends in zeros, the wrapped taps point at padded zeros, and the circular result is the linear list $\{2,8,15,\dots,4,1\}$. The zeros are not data; they are room for the tail. (In Part III padding bought finer DTFT samples; here it buys correctness.) ```fig dft-padded ``` ## The filtering recipe **Fast filtering with the DFT** (input length $L$, filter length $M$): 1. Choose $N\ge L+M-1$ and zero-pad both $x$ and $h$ to length $N$. 2. Compute $X[k]$ and $H[k]$ ($N$-point DFTs). 3. Multiply bin by bin: $Y[k]=X[k]H[k]$. 4. Invert: $y[n]=\text{IDFT}\{Y\}$; its first $L+M-1$ samples are the linear convolution. *Honest accounting:* each direct DFT costs about $N^2$ multiplications, so today this loses to the direct $L\cdot M$ sum. The transform is the bottleneck, and the FFT (next topic) removes it. ## Exam pointers - Know all three bridges: $X[k]=Na_k$, $c_k=X[k]/T_0$, $X[k]=X(e^{j2\pi k/N})$. - When computing a small DFT by hand, write the $W_N^{kn}$ table first. - Bin $k$ in hertz: $f_k=kf_s/N$ for $k\le N/2$, $(k-N)f_s/N$ above; resolution $1/T_0$. - Choosing $T_s$ and $T_0$: $T_s<\frac1{2B}$ against aliasing; $T_0$ long enough for the resolution you need and to cover the signal (avoid leakage); $N=T_0/T_s$ a power of 2 for the FFT, using zero-padding if necessary.
